entities.name: Church of God in Christ
entities.label: Institution
entities.summary:
The Church of God in Christ (COGIC), founded 1897 in Mississippi by Charles Harrison Mason and Charles Price Jones as a Holiness church, and reconstituted as a Pentecostal denomination in 1907 after Mason attended the Azusa Street Revival and returned speaking in tongues, is the largest African American Pentecostal denomination in the world — with 6.5 million members in 12,000 congregations in the United States and international presence in 60 countries. COGIC is the single largest African American Christian denomination.

Charles Harrison Mason (1866-1961) — born to freed slaves in Tennessee, ordained in 1893, and co-founded the Church of God in Christ in 1897 — attended the Azusa Street Revival in Los Angeles in 1907. Returning to Memphis speaking in tongues, he reconstituted COGIC as a Pentecostal church; his co-founder Jones refused Pentecostal theology and separated. Mason led COGIC for 54 years — one of the longest single-person denominational leaderships in American history.

COGIC's historical significance: because Mason had obtained a legal church charter (most white Pentecostal ministers had not), COGIC ordination was legally valid for World War I ministerial exemptions — many white Pentecostal ministers sought COGIC ordination to avoid draft, creating an unusual interracial religious dependency during a period of intense segregation. COGIC produced gospel music traditions that fed into soul and rock and roll: Aretha Franklin's father was a COGIC minister; Sister Rosetta Tharpe (COGIC) pioneered electric guitar gospel that influenced rock and roll.

historicalSignificance.significanceNarrative: The Church of God in Christ — producing Sister Rosetta Tharpe's electric guitar gospel that pioneered rock and roll, creating an interracial religious dependency through WWI draft exemptions, and becoming the world's largest African American denomination — is the most culturally consequential African American religious institution in American musical and social history.
